page: Amazon Web Services m4.10xlarge is a general-purpose virtual server deployed on the Xen hypervisor. The hardware profile is driven by Intel Xeon E5-2676 v3 processors based on the x86_64 architecture, delivering 20 physical cores and 40 vCPUs at a base clock speed of 2.4 GHz. Memory capacity totals 160.0 GB of RAM, maintaining a balanced 1:4 allocation of 4.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated GPU hardware or local NVMe storage, meaning persistent storage requirements rely entirely on external network-attached volumes. Baseline network connectivity provides a throughput limit of 10 Gbps.

Performance benchmarks illustrate a stark division between single-thread efficiency and aggregate multi-thread capacity. Driven by older architecture without modern vector extensions such as AVX-512, single-core metrics fall into the bottom 25% of tested systems, including a Geekbench single-core score of 1080.0 and stress-ng single-core rating of 1243.98. Conversely, multi-threaded workloads demonstrate solid middle-tier output, represented by a multi-core Geekbench score of 9510.0, a PassMark CPU score of 28983.81, and 29.88 million Redis SET operations per second.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the m4.10xlarge trades raw instruction throughput per core for substantial parallel CPU and memory volume. Without bundled local disk resources, workloads needing high storage performance incur additional storage overhead. The configuration suits high-concurrency general-purpose computing, enterprise application backends, mid-sized relational database hosting, and distributed batch processing tasks that can scale horizontally across 40 dedicated threads without relying on peak per-core frequency.
description: Amazon Web Services m4.10xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine featuring an Intel Xeon E5-2676 v3 processor running on the x86_64 architecture. It provides 40 vCPUs across 20 physical cores clocked at 2.4 GHz, paired with 160.0 GB of system RAM at a balanced 1:4 allocation ratio. The instance includes no bundled local storage or GPU hardware accelerators, relying on a 10 Gbps baseline network link for storage and data interconnects. Benchmark results demonstrate average multi-core compute and memory bandwidth alongside lower-tier single-core instruction speeds, reflecting its legacy hardware architecture. While single-threaded performance is restrained, the high core count and ample memory footprint make it a viable, cost-balanced option for parallel batch processing, multi-threaded web serving, distributed caching with Redis, and general enterprise application deployments.
